items.prompt: In a fair test, how many things should you change?

options.why: If you change two things, you cannot tell which one made the difference.
Changing everything makes the results impossible to compare.
You need to change one thing to see what it does.

hints: Think about how you would know what caused a result.
If two things change, can you tell which one mattered?
Find the smallest number that still lets you test something.
items.explanation: In a fair test you change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know that one thing caused any difference.

items.prompt: Match each measuring tool to what it measures.
hints: Each tool measures one thing.
Think about where you have seen each tool used.
Start with the stopwatch. What do you use it for in a race?
items.explanation: A ruler measures length, a thermometer measures temperature and a measuring jug measures volume. A stopwatch measures time and a forcemeter measures force.

items.prompt: What temperature does the thermometer show?

figure.alt: A thermometer from 0 to 50 °C, marked every 5 degrees. The liquid reaches the line for 35 °C.

hints: Look at the top of the liquid.
Count the marks between the numbers to see what each mark means.
Find the numbered line just below the top of the liquid.
items.explanation: The liquid stops at the line halfway between 30 and 40, so the temperature is 35 °C.

items.prompt: How much water is in the measuring jug?

figure.alt: A measuring jug marked every 50 ml up to 1000 ml. The water is level with the 450 ml mark.

hints: Read the scale at the top of the water.
Work out what each small mark is worth.
Find the numbered mark just below the water, then count on.
items.explanation: Each mark is 50 ml. The water is one mark above 400 ml, so there is 450 ml.

figure.alt: A leaf next to a ruler. The leaf starts at the 2 cm mark and ends at the 9 cm mark.

hints: Look at where the leaf starts. Is it at zero?
Length is the distance from one end to the other.
Find the end mark, then take away the start mark.
items.explanation: The leaf goes from 2 cm to 9 cm. 9 take away 2 is 7, so the leaf is 7 cm long.

items.prompt: Sam wants to find out which ball bounces highest. What is the fair way to test this?

options.text: Drop the light balls from higher up.
options.why: Every ball should start from the same height, or the test is not fair.

options.text: Drop each ball onto a different floor.
options.why: The floor could change the bounce. Keep it the same.

options.text: Throw some balls and drop the others.
options.why: Throwing adds a push. Every ball should be dropped the same way.

options.text: Drop each ball from the same height onto the same floor.

hints: Only the ball should change.
List the things that could change a bounce.
Check each answer: does it change anything except the ball?
items.explanation: Only the type of ball should change. Dropping every ball from the same height onto the same floor keeps the test fair.

items.prompt: Maya has not done her test yet. She says, 'I think the car will roll further on wood.' What is this?

options.why: A result is what you find after the test.
A conclusion is what you decide after looking at the results.
A measurement uses a tool and a unit, like cm.

hints: Maya has not done the test yet.
Think about which word means saying what you think will happen.
Look for the word that happens before a test.
items.explanation: A prediction says what you think will happen before you test. Maya can check her prediction when she gets her results.

items.prompt: Which unit is best for measuring the length of a classroom?

options.why: Millilitres measure volume, like water in a jug.
Kilograms measure mass, or how heavy something is.
Degrees Celsius measure temperature.

hints: Length is how long something is.
Think about which units go with a ruler or a measuring tape.
A classroom is much longer than a ruler.
items.explanation: Metres measure length. A classroom is several metres long, so metres are the best unit.

items.prompt: Ayu tests if the amount of water changes how tall cress grows. Choose 2 things she must keep the same.

options.why: This is the one thing she changes.
This is what she measures at the end.

hints: Find the one thing Ayu changes.
Find the thing she measures at the end.
Everything else must stay the same.
items.explanation: Ayu changes only the amount of water and measures the height. The seed type and the light must stay the same to make it fair.

items.prompt: Why is it a good idea to repeat a measurement?

options.text: to make the test take longer
options.why: Repeating is not about time. It helps you trust your results.

options.text: to change the thing you are testing
options.why: In a repeat, you do exactly the same test again.

options.text: to check that you get a similar result
so you can pick the result you like
options.why: Scientists use every result, even the ones they did not expect.

hints: Mistakes can happen in any test.
What would you learn if the second result was very different?
Think about how repeating helps you trust a result.
items.explanation: Repeating a measurement checks that the results are similar. If one result is very different, you may have made a mistake.

items.prompt: Plan a fair test to find which paper towel soaks up the most water.

criteria.label: Says what to change: the type of paper towel
Names 2 things to keep the same
Says what to measure and gives a unit

planning: What will you keep the same?
What will you measure, and with what tool?
items.model: I will change the type of paper towel. I will keep the size of each towel, the amount of water and the time the same. I will dip each towel in 100 ml of water for 10 seconds. Then I will measure how much water is left with a measuring jug.
hints: Start with the one thing you will change.
Think about the water, the towel size and the time.
Say how you will measure the water that is soaked up.
items.explanation: Change only the type of paper towel. Keep the towel size, amount of water and time the same, then measure the water soaked up in millilitres.

items.prompt: Kiko grows a bean in sandy soil on a sunny windowsill. Another grows in garden soil in a dark corner. The first grows taller. Can she say sandy soil is better?

options.text: Yes, because the bean in sandy soil grew taller.
options.why: That bean also had more light. The light might be the reason.

options.text: Yes, because sandy soil is always best.
options.why: Different plants grow well in different soils. Her test was not fair.

options.text: No, because beans cannot grow on windowsills.
options.why: Beans can grow on a windowsill if they get water and light.

options.text: No, because she changed both the soil and the light.

hints: Count how many things were different between the two beans.
In a fair test only one thing changes.
Compare the two places. Are they the same?
items.explanation: Kiko changed two things: the soil and the amount of light. She cannot tell which one made the bean grow taller.
